chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Advance Tax Is and Why It Exists

lessons.title: Advance Tax, TDS and Self-Assessment Tax: How the Three Fit Together

body.text: You have one income tax bill for the year, and three ways of paying it. TDS is deducted by others, advance tax is paid by you during the year, and self-assessment tax is paid by you after the year ends. When you file your return, the three are simply added up and checked against the bill.

children.text: Most confusion about advance tax comes from treating TDS, advance tax and self-assessment tax as three different taxes. They are not. They are three payment routes into the same account, all credited against your PAN. Once you see them as one bill paid in three ways, the rest of this course is just timing and arithmetic.

markDefs.definition: Tax deducted at source by whoever pays you, deposited in your name and PAN. It is a credit against your final tax, not a separate tax.
Tax you estimate and pay yourself in instalments during the tax year on income not fully covered by TDS.
The balance of tax, along with any interest, that you pay after the tax year ends and before filing your income tax return. Section 286 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (old section 140A).

body.text: TDS is not your final tax. It is a flat-rate deposit made on a single stream of income by someone who knows nothing about the rest of your finances. A bank deducts 10% on FD interest whether your slab is 5% or 30%. The gap between that deposit and your real tax is exactly what advance tax is designed to fill.

children.text: Following One Taxpayer Through a Full Year
Neha is a 34-year-old analyst at a financial services firm in Mumbai, on the new tax regime. For tax year 2026-27 her income has four parts, and each part meets TDS differently.

body.caption: Neha's income and TDS for tax year 2026-27

cells: Her employer deducts monthly on salary after the ₹75,000 standard deduction
Dividend on ITC shares in her Zerodha demat
10% because dividend from one company crossed ₹10,000
Short-term gain on Tata Motors shares held 7 months
No TDS on capital gains for a resident individual

body.title: Show me the math: Neha's actual tax for the year

children.text: Salary after standard deduction is ₹29,25,000. Add FD interest and dividend, which are taxed at slab rates, and her slab income is ₹30,60,000. The short-term gain on listed shares is taxed separately at a flat 20%.

content.caption: From slab tax to total tax

cells: Slab tax on salary, interest and dividend

children.text: Her total income is well above ₹12 lakh, so there is no rebate, and below ₹50 lakh, so there is no surcharge.

body.label: Tax still due after all TDS
body.context: Total tax of ₹5,38,720 minus TDS of ₹4,89,300. Because this is ₹10,000 or more, Neha is liable to pay advance tax.

body.title: Quick Check: The FD Gap
body.question: Neha's bank deducted ₹12,000 of TDS on her ₹1,20,000 of FD interest. Her income is taxed at the 30% slab. How much more tax does she owe on that interest beyond the TDS, including 4% cess?
options: Nil, TDS has already been deducted
body.explanation: Her real tax on the interest is 30% of ₹1,20,000, which is ₹36,000, plus 4% cess, giving ₹37,440. The bank has already deducted ₹12,000, so ₹25,440 is still owed. ₹37,440 is the full tax, not the balance. This gap is the most common reason salaried people with large FDs end up owing advance tax.

children.text: During the year Neha pays ₹45,000 as advance tax across the instalment dates, based on her best estimate. After 31 March, her AIS shows slightly more interest than she had expected, and her final figures leave a balance.

body.title: Try It: Neha's Balancing Payment
body.prompt: Neha's total tax is ₹5,38,720. TDS credited to her is ₹4,89,300 and she has paid ₹45,000 as advance tax. Ignoring interest, how much self-assessment tax must she pay before filing her return? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: ₹5,38,720 minus ₹4,89,300 of TDS leaves ₹49,420. Subtracting ₹45,000 of advance tax leaves ₹4,420 as self-assessment tax. Because her advance tax covered at least 90% of the tax due after TDS, the interest for not paying advance tax does not apply, though interest for short instalments may still apply depending on when she paid. Chapter 4 covers both.

body.title: How Neha's ₹5,38,720 tax bill was actually paid

children.text: Notice the proportions. Around 88% of Neha's tax was handled by her employer without her lifting a finger. Yet the remaining ₹49,420 was entirely her responsibility, and that small slice is where interest and notices come from.
Both are paid by you, through the same e-Pay Tax service on the portal, into the same PAN. The difference is timing, and timing decides whether interest applies.

body.title: Same payment screen, very different consequences

columns.label: Advance tax (minor head 100)
points: Paid during the tax year, by 31 March at the latest
Based on your estimate of the full year's income
Paid on time and in full, it attracts no interest
Meant to cover income that TDS does not fully reach

columns.label: Self-assessment tax (minor head 300)
points: Paid after 31 March, before you file the return
Any interest for missed advance tax is added and must be paid with it
Meant to settle the small final difference, not replace advance tax

body.text: Choosing the wrong type of payment on the challan is a common and avoidable mistake. The money is not lost, because it is still credited to your PAN, but it may not be treated as the payment you intended. The e-filing portal lets you request a correction to the type of payment or the tax head once, within 30 days of the challan date, under Services and then Challan Correction. After that, you have to approach your jurisdictional Assessing Officer.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Right Code
body.textWithBlank: When paying tax after the tax year has ended, to settle the final balance before filing your return, you select minor head ___ on the e-Pay Tax screen.
body.explanation: Minor head 300 is self-assessment tax. Minor head 100 is advance tax, used during the tax year. Minor head 400 is for paying a demand raised by the department after processing or assessment.

body.title: Scenario: Farhan Picks the Wrong Code
body.scenario: Farhan, a Kolkata-based freelance video editor, estimates ₹60,000 of tax for tax year 2026-27. On 12 December 2026 he pays ₹60,000 online, but in a hurry selects "Self-Assessment Tax (300)" instead of "Advance Tax (100)". He notices the mistake on 5 January 2027 while downloading the challan receipt for his records.
body.prompt: Has Farhan lost his money? What could go wrong if he ignores the mistake, and what should he do now?
body.modelAnswer: The money is not lost. It is credited to his PAN and will show in his tax credit statement. The risk is in how it is treated: a payment coded as self-assessment tax made during the year may not be matched against his advance tax instalments, which can lead to a mismatch when his return is processed and an interest demand he then has to dispute. He is still within 30 days of the 12 December challan date, so he should log in to the e-filing portal, go to Services and then Challan Correction, and request a change of the type of payment from 300 to 100. The correction can be requested only once, so he should also check that the year selected on the challan is right before submitting. If he misses the 30-day window, he would have to write to his jurisdictional Assessing Officer, which is slower.

body.title: Your End-of-Year Reconciliation Routine
steps: Download Form 16 from your employer and every Form 16A from banks and companies that deducted TDS
Open AIS on the e-filing portal and match each TDS entry to the corresponding Form 16 or 16A
Open Form 26AS and confirm every advance tax challan appears with the correct type of payment and year
Add all income from AIS and your own records, including capital gains from your broker's tax P&L statement on Zerodha Console or similar
Compute total tax, subtract TDS, TCS and advance tax, and pay any remaining balance as self-assessment tax under minor head 300
Enter every advance tax and self-assessment tax challan in Schedule IT of your return before filing

cards.definition: Tax withheld by the payer of your income and credited to your PAN. A credit against your final tax, not the final tax itself.
Tax you pay yourself during the tax year on estimated income. Minor head 100 on the challan.
The balance of tax and interest paid after the year ends and before filing. Section 286 (old 140A). Minor head 300.
The challan code for paying a tax demand raised by the department after processing or assessment.
Your tax credit statement, showing TDS, TCS and tax paid through challans against your PAN.
Annual Information Statement. A wider record of your reported income and transactions, including TDS, interest, dividends and securities sales.
The part of the income tax return where you list advance tax and self-assessment tax challans.
A code identifying the bank branch through which a tax payment was received. Together with the date and challan serial number, it identifies your challan.

points: TDS, advance tax and self-assessment tax are three ways of paying one tax bill, all credited to your PAN
Self-assessment tax is the balancing figure: total tax plus interest, minus TDS, TCS and advance tax
TDS is a flat-rate deposit on individual incomes, so it often falls short for people in higher slabs
Advance tax uses minor head 100 and is paid during the year; self-assessment tax uses minor head 300 and is paid after it ends
A wrong challan code can be corrected once on the portal within 30 days of the challan date
Before filing, match TDS, advance tax and self-assessment tax against AIS and Form 26AS, then report challans in Schedule IT

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Section references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025, with the corresponding Income-tax Act, 1961 section in brackets. Examples use new regime rates and thresholds for tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing, which can change with each Union Budget. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
